fields.title: The Gospel of John
fields.subtitle: The Open Word Bible, with an Introduction and Conclusion
fields.description: The fourth Gospel, which begins before the beginning — “In the beginning was the Word” — and says plainly why it was written: so that you may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and by believing have life in his name. Seven signs, from water turned to wine to Lazarus called out of the tomb; seven “I am” sayings; Nicodemus by night and the Samaritan woman at noon; the farewell in the upper room; the cross as the hour of glory; and breakfast by the lake. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the Gospel of John?
qa.answer: The fourth of the four Gospels, the accounts of the life, death and resurrection of Jesus in the New Testament. Roughly nine-tenths of it has no parallel in Matthew, Mark or Luke: only John tells of the wedding at Cana, Nicodemus, the woman at the well, the raising of Lazarus, the washing of the disciples’ feet and Thomas touching the wounds. It states its own purpose in 20:31 — that its readers may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and by believing have life in his name.

qa.question: Who wrote the Gospel of John?
qa.answer: The Gospel does not name its author. It points to “the disciple whom Jesus loved” and says his testimony stands behind the book (21:24). From the second century the church identified him as John the son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve, writing late in life at Ephesus, probably toward the end of the first century. Some scholars think the beloved disciple was a follower of Jesus outside the Twelve, or that his own disciples gave the book its final form.

qa.question: What are the seven signs in John?
qa.answer: John calls Jesus’s miracles signs, deeds that point beyond themselves. The seven are water turned into wine at Cana, an official’s son healed, a man ill for thirty-eight years made to walk, five thousand fed, Jesus walking on the water, a man born blind given sight, and Lazarus raised from the dead. Each is paired with words that explain it, as the feeding of the crowd is followed by “I am the bread of life”.

qa.question: What are the “I am” sayings in John?
qa.answer: Seven sayings in which Jesus describes himself: the bread of life, the light of the world, the door, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life, the way, the truth and the life, and the true vine. John also records Jesus saying “I am” with nothing after it, as in “before Abraham was, I am” (8:58), which echoes the name God gave Moses at the burning bush.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

qa.question: Why is the story of the woman caught in adultery set apart?
qa.answer: The passage (7:53–8:11) is not found in the oldest manuscripts of John, and later manuscripts place it in different spots. Like most Bibles, this edition prints it, set apart and in brackets, with a note saying why.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

— John 1:1

Every other Gospel begins somewhere on a map. Mark begins at the Jordan, Matthew with a family tree, Luke in the temple at Jerusalem. John begins before there was a map at all. His first three words are the first three words of the Bible, “In the beginning”, and before he has told us a single thing Jesus did, he has told us who Jesus is: the Word who was with God, and was God, and through whom everything that exists was made.

That is the key to the whole book. John is not less interested in what happened than the other Gospel writers; he is often more precise about times, places and festivals than any of them. But he will not let us watch a single scene without knowing who is standing in it. When Jesus turns water into wine, or gives sight to a blind man, or stands weeping at a friend’s grave, the reader already knows what the people in the story are only beginning to guess. The tension of the book lies in watching them find out, or refuse to.

Christians have loved this Gospel above the others for as long as there have been four. It has been called the “spiritual Gospel”, and it is the one most often put into the hands of someone reading the Bible for the first time. Both are fitting. It is simple enough that a child can follow it and deep enough that no one has ever reached the bottom of it. Its vocabulary is tiny, a few dozen ordinary words used over and over: light, life, love, truth, world, glory, believe, remain. But John turns those words slowly, like a jeweller turning a stone, until each one catches a different light.

Why a fourth Gospel?

Readers who come to John from Matthew, Mark and Luke notice at once how much is missing. There is no birth in Bethlehem, no baptism scene, no temptation in the wilderness. Jesus tells no parables of the kind the other Gospels are full of: no sower, no prodigal son, no good Samaritan. He casts out no demons. At the last supper there is no bread and cup; instead, Jesus kneels with a towel and washes his disciples’ feet.

And readers notice how much is new. Roughly nine-tenths of John has no parallel in the other three. Only John tells of the wedding at Cana, the conversation with Nicodemus by night, the woman at the well, the man who had been ill for thirty-eight years, the man born blind, the raising of Lazarus, the long farewell in the upper room, Thomas putting his hand into the wounds, and breakfast on the beach. Where the others give us mostly short sayings, John gives us long conversations and speeches, in which a single image (bread, water, light, a shepherd, a vine) is turned over until it has given up its meaning.

The early church explained the difference simply. Around AD 200, Clement of Alexandria wrote that John, seeing that the outward facts had already been set down in the other Gospels, composed “a spiritual Gospel”. That is not quite right, since John is full of outward facts, but it points in the right direction. John writes for readers who already know the story and need to understand it.

The book says why it was written

Most books leave their purpose to be guessed. John states his near the end, plainly:

These, though, are written down so that you may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and by believing have life in his name.

— John 20:31

Everything in the book serves that sentence. The word to watch is believe. John never once uses the noun “faith”; he uses the verb, nearly a hundred times, more than Matthew, Mark and Luke together. For John, faith is not something you have so much as something you do: a movement of the whole person toward Jesus. People in this Gospel come to Jesus, follow him, remain in him, eat and drink him (in his own startling words in chapter 6). Each is another way of saying believe.

And belief, in John, is rarely instant. One of the quiet pleasures of reading the book through is watching people move toward Jesus by stages. Nicodemus comes “at night” in chapter 3, cautious and puzzled. In chapter 7 he speaks up, carefully, in Jesus’s defence before the council. In chapter 19, after the crucifixion, when the disciples have scattered, he comes out in daylight carrying about seventy pounds of myrrh and aloes to bury the body. The man born blind in chapter 9 calls Jesus first “the man named Jesus”, then “a prophet”, then a man “from God”, and at last falls down to worship him. John is showing his readers that it is possible to start a long way off and still arrive.

Seven signs

John never calls Jesus’s miracles “miracles” or “mighty works”. He calls them signs, deeds that point past themselves to something greater. The first half of the book is built around seven of them:

  • Water into wine at a wedding in Cana (2:1–11): the old purification jars filled to the brim with the best wine, kept until last.
  • An official’s son healed at a distance, by a word (4:46–54).
  • A man ill for thirty-eight years made to walk at the pool of Bethesda (5:1–15), on a Sabbath.
  • Five thousand fed from five barley loaves and two fish (6:1–15), followed by the teaching on the bread of life.
  • Walking on the water to his frightened disciples (6:16–21).
  • A man born blind given sight (9:1–41), after which the blind man sees and the sighted religious leaders are shown to be blind.
  • Lazarus raised after four days in the tomb (11:1–44).

The order is not accidental. The signs grow larger as they go, from a household embarrassment at a wedding to the undoing of death itself, and each is paired with words that explain it. Jesus feeds a crowd and then says he is the bread; he opens blind eyes and then says he is the light; he calls Lazarus out of the grave and then says he is the resurrection. The sign is the picture; the saying is the caption. The last sign is also the one that sets the authorities on the path to the cross: from the day Lazarus walks out of his tomb, John tells us, they planned to kill Jesus. Giving life costs Jesus his own.

Many readers have seen an eighth sign standing behind the seven: the empty tomb, on “the first day of the week”, which no one witnesses and to which the whole book points.

“I am”

Alongside the signs runs the other great thread of the book, the sayings in which Jesus describes himself with the words “I am”:

  • “I am the bread of life” (6:35)
  • “I am the light of the world” (8:12)
  • “I am the door” (10:9)
  • “I am the good shepherd” (10:11)
  • “I am the resurrection and the life” (11:25)
  • “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (14:6)
  • “I am the true vine” (15:1)

Each takes something people could not live without (food, light, safety, guidance, life itself) and says that what they were really reaching for is a person. But John also records Jesus saying “I am” with nothing after it at all, and these are the moments when his hearers react most violently. In chapter 8, arguing about Abraham, he says, “before Abraham was, I am”, and they pick up stones. Any Jewish hearer would have caught the echo of the name God gave Moses at the burning bush, “I am who I am”. In the garden in chapter 18, soldiers come to arrest him; he asks who they are looking for, answers “I am he” (in Greek, simply “I am”), and they step backward and fall to the ground. In John, Jesus is never really the prisoner. He goes to his death, as he says himself, because he lays down his life of his own accord.

Light and darkness, night and noon

John’s prologue announces a contest: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it.” The rest of the book stages it, often through the simple detail of what time it is.

Nicodemus, a respected teacher of Israel, comes to Jesus at night, and leaves still in the dark about what Jesus means. In the very next chapter, a Samaritan woman with a damaged past meets Jesus at a well about noon, in the full light of day, and goes back to her town to tell everyone she has found the Messiah. The insider stays confused; the outsider becomes a witness. When Judas leaves the last supper to betray his master, John adds three words that are among the most chilling in Scripture: “And it was night.”

And on the morning of the resurrection, Mary Magdalene comes to the tomb “while it was still dark”, and leaves it having seen the Lord.

The festivals

Much of John is set in Jerusalem during the great feasts of Israel, and Jesus repeatedly takes the meaning of a festival into himself. At Passover he feeds the crowd with bread in the wilderness, as Israel was fed with manna. At the Festival of Tabernacles, when water was poured out at the temple and great lamps lit its courts, he stands and cries out that anyone thirsty should come to him and drink, and says, “I am the light of the world.” At the Festival of Dedication, which remembered the cleansing of the temple, he speaks of himself as the one the Father set apart and sent.

Above all, John frames the story with the Passover. At the start, John the Baptist points to Jesus and says, “Look, there is the Lamb of God, who carries away the sin of the world!” At the end, John notes that Jesus was condemned about noon on the day of Preparation for the Passover, the day the lambs for the feast were slaughtered; that a sponge of sour wine was lifted to him on hyssop, the plant used to mark the doorposts with blood in Egypt; and that not one of his bones was broken, as the law required of the Passover lamb. John does not stop to explain these details. He trusts his readers to notice.

The hour and the glory

Early in the book, Jesus keeps saying that his “hour” has not yet come. At Cana he says it to his mother; in Jerusalem the authorities try to seize him, but cannot, “because his hour had not yet come.” Then, in chapter 12, when some Greeks come asking to see him, he says, “The hour has come when the Son of Man is to be glorified”, and begins at once to speak of a grain of wheat falling into the ground and dying.

This is perhaps the most profound thing about John’s Gospel. The other Gospels show the cross as the depth of Jesus’s humiliation, followed by the glory of the resurrection. John sees glory in the cross itself. Jesus speaks of being “lifted up”, a phrase that means both raised on a cross and exalted to a throne. His last word from the cross is not a cry of abandonment but a single Greek word of completion:

When Jesus had taken the sour wine, he said, “It is finished.” Then he bowed his head and handed over his spirit.

— John 19:30

The love that John says Jesus had for his own, the love with which he “loved them to the end”, is shown nowhere more fully than there. In John, the cross is not where the glory of God is hidden. It is where it is seen.

What are you looking for?

Some of John’s meaning is carried by quiet repetitions that are easy to miss. The first words Jesus speaks in this Gospel are a question to two men who have started to follow him: “What are you looking for?” Near the end, standing outside his own empty tomb, he asks a weeping woman almost the same question: “Who is it you are looking for?” She supposes he is the gardener, until he says her name. The whole Gospel lies between those two questions.

Or take the fire. On the night of the arrest, Peter stands warming himself by a charcoal fire in the high priest’s courtyard, and that night he denies three times that he knows Jesus. The Greek word for that kind of fire appears only twice in the New Testament. The second time is in the last chapter of John, on the shore of Galilee, where the risen Jesus has a charcoal fire burning with fish laid on it, and asks Peter three times, “Do you love me?” Three denials on the night of one fire; three declarations of love beside another. Jesus does not merely forgive Peter. He takes him back to the place of his failure, and makes it the place of his calling: “Feed my sheep.”

The disciple whom Jesus loved

The Gospel never names its author. It points instead to a figure it calls “the disciple whom Jesus loved”, who leans against Jesus at the last supper, stands at the foot of the cross where Jesus entrusts his mother to him, outruns Peter to the empty tomb, and is the first to recognise the risen Lord on the shore. The closing verses say that his testimony stands behind the book: “This is the disciple who is testifying about these things and who has written them, and we know his testimony is true.”

From the second century onward, the church identified this disciple as John the son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve, writing late in a long life at Ephesus, probably toward the end of the first century. Many readers still hold that view; others think the beloved disciple was a follower of Jesus from Jerusalem outside the Twelve, or that his own disciples gave the book its final shape (the “we” of that closing verse). Either way, it is striking that the writer never puts himself at the centre. He is not named; he is simply loved. Perhaps that is the point. Every reader of this Gospel is invited to stand where he stood.

How to read John

John can be read in an afternoon, and it is worth reading that way at least once, straight through, to feel its shape: the prologue (1:1–18); the book of signs, in which Jesus reveals himself to the world and the world largely turns away (1:19–12:50); the farewell, in which he turns to his own and prepares them for his going (13–17); the hour of glory, his arrest, trial, death and resurrection (18–20); and the epilogue by the lake (21).

But it is also a book to read slowly. Notice who comes to Jesus and who goes away. Notice when it is night. Notice how often the people in the story misunderstand Jesus in exactly the way that lets him say more: Nicodemus wondering how a grown man can be born again, the Samaritan woman asking where the living water is kept, the disciples supposing Lazarus is only asleep. And notice the questions Jesus asks, because John means them for the reader too. “What are you looking for?” “Do you want to be well?” “Do you believe this?” “Do you love me?”

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in John are worth knowing about before you begin.

“The Jews.” John uses the phrase more than seventy times, in several senses: the Jewish people as a whole, the people of Judea, and very often the religious authorities in Jerusalem who opposed Jesus. Where the authorities are meant, this translation says “the Jewish leaders”. Jesus, his mother and every one of his first disciples were Jews, and nothing in this Gospel should be read as setting him against his own people.

John 3:16. The most famous verse in the Bible reads a little differently here: “For God’s love for the world was such that he gave his one and only Son.” The Greek word often translated “so” (“God so loved the world”) means “in this way”, not “so much”: the verse tells us not how much God loved but how, by giving.

The disputed passage. The story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11) is not found in the oldest manuscripts of John, and later manuscripts place it in different spots. Like most Bibles, this edition prints it, set apart and in brackets, with a note.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Greek beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

Where the authorities are meant, this translation says “the Jewish leaders”. Jesus, his mother and every one of his first disciples were Jews, and nothing in this Gospel should be read as setting him against his own people. John 3:16. The most famous verse in the Bible reads a little differently here: “For God’s love for the world was such that he gave his one and only Son.” The Greek word often translated “so” (“God so loved the world”) means “in this way”, not “so much”: the verse tells us not how much God loved but how, by giving. The disputed passage. The story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11) is not found in the oldest manuscripts of John, and later manuscripts place it in different spots. Like most Bibles, this edition prints it, set apart and in brackets, with a note. fields.title: John 1
fields.body_html:
The Word became flesh

In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was with God in the beginning. All things came into being through him, and without him nothing came into being that has come into being. In him was life, and that life was the light of all people. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it.

There came a man sent from God, whose name was John. He came as a witness, to testify about the light, so that through him everyone might believe. He himself was not the light; he came to testify about the light. The true light, who gives light to everyone, was coming into the world.

He was in the world, and though the world came into being through him, the world did not recognize him. He came to what was his own, and his own people did not receive him. But to all who received him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God— children born not of blood, nor of human desire, nor of a husband’s will, but born of God.

The Word became flesh and made his home among us. We have seen his glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth. John testified about him and cried out, “This is the one I meant when I said, ‘He who comes after me ranks ahead of me, because he existed before me.’” From his fullness we have all received grace upon grace. For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen God. The one and only Son, who is himself God and is close beside the Father, has made him known.

What John testified

This is what John testified when the Jewish leaders sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, “Who are you?” He spoke openly and did not refuse to answer; he stated plainly, “I am not the Christ.” So they asked him, “Then what? Are you Elijah?” He said, “I am not.”

“Are you the Prophet?” He answered, “No.” So they said to him, “Who are you, then? We have to give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?” John answered in the words of the prophet Isaiah: “I am a voice of someone calling out in the wilderness, ‘Make the road straight for the Lord.’”

They had been sent by the Pharisees. They questioned him further: “Why are you baptizing, then, if you are not the Christ, or Elijah, or the Prophet?” John answered them, “I baptize with water. But someone stands among you whom you do not know. He is the one who comes after me, and I am not worthy even to untie the strap of his sandal.” All this happened at Bethany on the east side of the Jordan River, where John was baptizing.

The Lamb of God

The next day John saw Jesus coming toward him and said, “Look, there is the Lamb of God, who carries away the sin of the world! This is the one I meant when I said, ‘A man who comes after me ranks ahead of me, because he existed before me.’ I myself did not know him, but I came baptizing with water so that he might be revealed to Israel.” John also gave this testimony: “I saw the Spirit come down from heaven like a dove and remain on him. I myself did not know him, but the one who sent me to baptize with water told me, ‘When you see the Spirit come down and remain on someone, that is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.’ I have seen it, and I have testified that this is the Chosen One of God.”

The first disciples

The next day John was there again with two of his disciples. He watched Jesus walking by and said, “Look, there is the Lamb of God!” The two disciples heard what he said, and they followed Jesus. Jesus turned and saw them following. He asked them, “What are you looking for?” They answered him, “Rabbi”—the word means Teacher—“where are you staying?” He said to them, “Come, and you will see.” So they went and saw where he was staying, and they spent the rest of that day with him. It was about four in the afternoon. Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, was one of the two who heard John’s words and followed Jesus. The first thing Andrew did was to find his brother Simon and tell him, “We have found the Messiah” (that is, the Christ). He brought Simon to Jesus. Jesus looked closely at him and said, “You are Simon, son of John. You will be called Cephas” (which means Peter, that is, Rock).

Philip and Nathanael

The next day Jesus decided to leave for Galilee. He found Philip and said to him, “Follow me.” Philip came from Bethsaida, the hometown of Andrew and Peter. Philip found Nathanael and told him, “Moses wrote about him in the law, and so did the prophets, and now we have found him: Jesus son of Joseph, from Nazareth.” Nathanael answered, “Can anything good be from a place like Nazareth?” Philip said to him, “Come and see.” When Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him, he said of him, “Here is a true Israelite: there is nothing deceitful in him.” Nathanael asked him, “How do you know me?” Jesus answered, “I saw you while you were still under the fig tree, before Philip called you.” Nathanael answered, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are Israel’s King!” Jesus replied, “Do you believe because I told you that I saw you under the fig tree? You will see greater things than that.” Then he said to him, “Truly, truly, I tell you all: you will see heaven standing open, and God’s angels going up and coming down on the Son of Man.”

fields.title: John 2
fields.body_html:
The wedding at Cana

On the third day a wedding was held at Cana in Galilee, and Jesus’s mother was there. Jesus had been invited to the wedding too, along with his disciples. When the wine gave out, Jesus’s mother said to him, “They have no wine left.” Jesus said to her, “Woman, is that a matter for you and me? My hour has not yet come.” His mother said to the servants, “Do as he tells you, whatever it is.” Six stone water jars stood there, kept for Jewish ritual washing; each held about 20 to 30 gallons. Jesus said to them, “Fill the jars with water.” They filled them up to the top. Then he said to them, “Now dip some out and carry it to the man in charge of the feast.” And they did. The man in charge of the feast tasted the water that had become wine. He had no idea where it had come from, though the servants who had drawn the water knew. He called the bridegroom over and said to him, “Every host sets out the good wine first, and the lesser wine once the guests are drunk. But you have kept back the good wine until now.” Jesus did this at Cana in Galilee as the first of the signs. In it he revealed his glory, and his disciples believed in him.

After this he went down to Capernaum, together with his mother, his brothers and his disciples. They did not stay there many days.

Jesus clears the temple

The Jewish festival of Passover was approaching, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. In the temple courts he found people selling cattle, sheep and doves, and money changers sitting there. He made a whip out of cords and drove them all out of the temple courts, sheep and cattle alike. He spilled the money changers’ coins and turned their tables over. To the dove sellers he said, “Take all this away from here! Do not make my Father’s house a house of business.” His disciples remembered that it is written: “Zeal for your house will devour me.” The Jewish leaders then said to him, “What sign do you show us to justify doing these things?” Jesus replied, “Tear this temple down, and I will raise it up again within three days.” The Jewish leaders said, “Forty-six years this temple has been under construction, and you will raise it up in three days?” But the temple he meant was his own body. Later, when he had been raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and what Jesus had said.

During the Passover festival, while he was in Jerusalem, many came to believe in his name as they watched the signs he was doing. But Jesus, for his part, would not trust himself to them, because he knew all people. He did not need anyone to testify to him about people, for he himself knew what was in a person.

fields.title: John 3
fields.body_html:
Jesus and Nicodemus

Now there was a man named Nicodemus, a Pharisee and one of the leaders of the Jewish people. He came to Jesus at night and said to him, “Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher, because no one can do such signs as you do unless God is with them.” Jesus answered him, “Truly, truly, I tell you, unless someone is born from above, they cannot see the kingdom of God.” Nicodemus said to him, “How can a man be born once he has grown old? He cannot go back into his mother’s womb and be born a second time, can he?” Jesus replied, “Truly, truly, I tell you, unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, they cannot enter the kingdom of God. Whatever is born of the flesh is flesh, and whatever is born of the Spirit is spirit. Do not be surprised that I told you, ‘All of you must be born from above.’ The wind blows where it wants to. You hear its sound, yet you do not know where it has come from or where it is heading. That is how it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.” Nicodemus asked him, “How can this be possible?” Jesus answered, “You are the teacher of Israel, and yet you do not understand this? Truly, truly, I tell you, we speak of what we know and testify to what we have seen, and still you people do not accept our testimony. If you do not believe when I tell you about things on earth, how will you believe when I tell you about things in heaven? No one has gone up into heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son of Man. Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, and in the same way the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that everyone who believes will have eternal life in him.

For God’s love for the world was such that he gave his one and only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life. For God sent the Son into the world, not to condemn the world, but so that through him the world might be saved. The one who believes in him is not condemned, but the one who does not believe is condemned already, for not having believed in the name of the one and only Son of God. And this is how the judgment falls: the light has come into the world, but people loved the darkness more than the light, because the things they did were evil. For anyone who does what is wrong hates the light and will not come near it, so that what they do will not be exposed. But whoever practices the truth comes to the light, so that it may become plain that their deeds have been done in God.”

John points to Jesus

After this, Jesus went with his disciples into the Judean countryside. There he stayed with them for a while and baptized people. John too was baptizing, at Aenon near Salim, where there was plenty of water, and people kept coming to be baptized. This was before John had been put in prison.

Then a dispute broke out between some of John’s disciples and a Jewish man about ritual cleansing. They came to John and said to him, “Rabbi, the man who was with you on the other side of the Jordan, the one you testified about: look, he is baptizing, and everyone is going to him.” John replied, “No one can receive anything at all unless it has been given them from heaven. You yourselves are my witnesses that I said, ‘I am not the Christ; rather, I have been sent ahead of him.’ It is the bridegroom who has the bride. But the bridegroom’s friend, who stands by and listens for him, rejoices with great joy at the sound of the bridegroom’s voice. This, then, is my joy, and it has been made complete. He must grow greater, but I must grow less.

The one who comes from above

The one who comes from above is greater than all. Whoever is from the earth is earthly and speaks from an earthly point of view. The one who comes from heaven is greater than all. What he has seen and heard is what he bears witness to, but no one accepts his testimony. Anyone who accepts his testimony has put their seal on this: God is true. For the one God sent speaks the words of God, since the Spirit he gives is not measured out. The Father loves the Son and has handed everything over to him. Anyone who believes in the Son has eternal life, but anyone who refuses to obey the Son will not see life. Instead, the wrath of God remains on them.”

fields.title: John 4
fields.body_html:
Jesus and the Samaritan woman

Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that he was making and baptizing more disciples than John. (In fact it was not Jesus himself who baptized, but his disciples.) So he left Judea and went back once more to Galilee. He had to pass through Samaria. So he came to a Samaritan town called Sychar, near the piece of land that Jacob had given to his son Joseph. Jacob’s well was there. Jesus was worn out from the journey, so he sat down by the well just as he was. It was about noon.

A Samaritan woman came to draw water. Jesus said to her, “Give me a drink.” His disciples had gone off into the town to buy food. The Samaritan woman said to him, “How is it that a Jew like you asks a Samaritan woman like me for a drink?” (Jews do not use the same vessels as Samaritans.) Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift God gives, and who it is that says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ it is you who would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.” The woman said to him, “Sir, you have no bucket, and the well is deep. So where would this living water of yours come from? Surely you are not greater than our father Jacob? He gave us this well, and he and his sons and his animals all drank from it.” Jesus answered her, “All who drink this water will get thirsty again. But no one who drinks the water I will give will ever be thirsty again. The water I give will become in them a spring whose water leaps up into eternal life.” The woman said to him, “Sir, give me this water! Then I will not be thirsty, and I will be spared the trip out here to draw water.”

He told her, “Go and call your husband, and come back here.” The woman answered, “I do not have a husband.” Jesus said to her, “You are right to say, ‘I do not have a husband.’ In fact, you have had five husbands, and the one you are with now is not your husband. You have told the truth there.” The woman said to him, “Sir, I can see that you are a prophet. This mountain is where our ancestors worshiped; yet you Jews say that Jerusalem is the place where worship must be offered.” Jesus said to her, “Believe me, Woman: an hour is coming when your worship of the Father will not be on this mountain, nor in Jerusalem either. Your people worship without knowing what they worship; we know what we worship, since salvation comes from the Jews. But an hour is coming, and in fact it has already begun, when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth; for the Father is seeking people like these to worship him. God is spirit, and anyone who worships him has to do it in spirit and truth.” The woman said to him, “I know that Messiah is coming” (the one called the Christ). “When he comes, he will make everything plain to us.” Jesus said to her, “I am he, the one who is speaking with you.”

At that moment his disciples arrived, and they were astonished that he was speaking with a woman. Yet none of them said, “What are you looking for?” or, “Why are you speaking with her?” Then the woman left her water jar, went back into the town and said to the people, “Come and see a man who told me everything I have done. Could this possibly be the Christ?” The people went out of the town and began making their way to him.

Fields ready for harvest

Meanwhile the disciples kept urging him, “Rabbi, eat something.” But he said to them, “I have food to eat that you are not aware of.” So the disciples said to one another, “Nobody has brought him food, have they?” Jesus said to them, “My food is doing the will of the one who sent me, and bringing his work to completion.” “Do you not say, ‘Four months more, and the harvest will be here’? Listen, I tell you: raise your eyes and look at the fields. They have turned white, ready for harvest. Already the reaper is being paid and is gathering a crop for eternal life, so that the sower may rejoice along with the reaper. For here the saying proves true: ‘The sower is one person, and the reaper another.’ I sent you to reap what you did not labor over. Others did the labor, and you have taken up where their work left off.”

Many Samaritans believe

Many of the Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the woman’s word, as she testified, “He told me everything I have done.” When the Samaritans reached him, they kept asking him to stay with them, and he stayed there for two days. Because of his own word many more came to believe. They said to the woman, “It is no longer your report that makes us believe. We have listened to him ourselves, and we know that he is indeed the Savior of the world.”

Jesus heals an official’s son

After the two days he left there for Galilee. Jesus himself had declared that a prophet is not honored in his own homeland. So when he arrived in Galilee, the Galileans welcomed him. They had seen all that he had done in Jerusalem at the festival, since they too had been there for it.

So he went back to Cana in Galilee, the place where he had changed the water into wine. There was a royal official whose son lay ill at Capernaum. Hearing that Jesus had arrived in Galilee from Judea, he went to him and kept pleading with him to come down and heal his son, because the boy was dying. Jesus answered him, “None of you will believe unless you see signs and wonders.” The official pleaded, “Sir, come down before my little boy dies.” Jesus told him, “Go. Your son lives.” The man believed what Jesus had said to him and started for home. While he was still on the way down, his servants met him with the news that his boy was alive. So he asked them at what time the boy had begun to recover, and they told him, “The fever left him yesterday at about one in the afternoon.” Then the father realized that it had happened at the very hour Jesus had said to him, “Your son lives.” So he came to believe, together with all his household. Jesus did this, his second sign, after he had come back from Judea to Galilee.

(In fact it was not Jesus himself who baptized, but his disciples.) So he left Judea and went back once more to Galilee. He had to pass through Samaria. So he came to a Samaritan town called Sychar, near the piece of land that Jacob had given to his son Joseph. Jacob’s well was there. Jesus was worn out from the journey, so he sat down by the well just as he was. It was about noon. A Samaritan woman came to draw water. Jesus said to her, “Give me a drink.” His disciples had gone off into the town to buy food. The Samaritan woman said to him, “How is it that a Jew like you asks a Samaritan woman like me for a drink?” (Jews do not use the same vessels as Samaritans.) Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift God gives, and who it is that says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ it is you who would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.” The woman said to him, “Sir, you have no bucket, and the well is deep. So where would this living water of yours come from? Surely you are not greater than our father Jacob? He gave us this well, and he and his sons and his animals all drank from it.” Jesus answered her, “All who drink this water will get thirsty again. But no one who drinks the water I will give will ever be thirsty again. The water I give will become in them a spring whose water leaps up into eternal life.” The woman said to him, “Sir, give me this water! Then I will not be thirsty, and I will be spared the trip out here to draw water.” He told her, “Go and call your husband, and come back here.” The woman answered, “I do not have a husband.” Jesus said to her, “You are right to say, ‘I do not have a husband.’ In fact, you have had five husbands, and the one you are with now is not your husband. You have told the truth there.” The woman said to him, “Sir, I can see that you are a prophet. This mountain is where our ancestors worshiped; yet you Jews say that Jerusalem is the place where worship must be offered.” Jesus said to her, “Believe me, Woman: an hour is coming when your worship of the Father will not be on this mountain, nor in Jerusalem either. But an hour is coming, and in fact it has already begun, when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth; for the Father is seeking people like these to worship him. God is spirit, and anyone who worships him has to do it in spirit and truth.” The woman said to him, “I know that Messiah is coming” (the one called the Christ). “When he comes, he will make everything plain to us.” Jesus said to her, “I am he, the one who is speaking with you.” At that moment his disciples arrived, and they were astonished that he was speaking with a woman. Yet none of them said, “What are you looking for?” or, “Why are you speaking with her?” Then the woman left her water jar, went back into the town and said to the people, “Come and see a man who told me everything I have done. Could this possibly be the Christ?” The people went out of the town and began making their way to him. Fields ready for harvest Meanwhile the disciples kept urging him, “Rabbi, eat something.” But he said to them, “I have food to eat that you are not aware of.” So the disciples said to one another, “Nobody has brought him food, have they?” Jesus said to them, “My food is doing the will of the one who sent me, and bringing his work to completion.” “Do you not say, ‘Four months more, and the harvest will be here’? Listen, I tell you: raise your eyes and look at the fields. They have turned white, ready for harvest. Already the reaper is being paid and is gathering a crop for eternal life, so that the sower may rejoice along with the reaper. For here the saying proves true: ‘The sower is one person, and the reaper another.’ I sent you to reap what you did not labor over. We have listened to him ourselves, and we know that he is indeed the Savior of the world.” Jesus heals an official’s son After the two days he left there for Galilee. Jesus himself had declared that a prophet is not honored in his own homeland. So when he arrived in Galilee, the Galileans welcomed him. They had seen all that he had done in Jerusalem at the festival, since they too had been there for it. So he went back to Cana in Galilee, the place where he had changed the water into wine. There was a royal official whose son lay ill at Capernaum. Hearing that Jesus had arrived in Galilee from Judea, he went to him and kept pleading with him to come down and heal his son, because the boy was dying. Jesus answered him, “None of you will believe unless you see signs and wonders.” The official pleaded, “Sir, come down before my little boy dies.” Jesus told him, “Go. Your son lives.” The man believed what Jesus had said to him and started for home. While he was still on the way down, his servants met him with the news that his boy was alive. So he asked them at what time the boy had begun to recover, and they told him, “The fever left him yesterday at about one in the afternoon.” Then the father realized that it had happened at the very hour Jesus had said to him, “Your son lives.” So he came to believe, together with all his household. Jesus did this, his second sign, after he had come back from Judea to Galilee.

The healing at the pool

Some time after this there was a Jewish festival, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. In Jerusalem, by the Sheep Gate, there is a pool with five porticoes; in Hebrew it is called Bethesda. Many sick people used to lie in these porticoes: the blind, the lame and the paralyzed. One man there had been ill for thirty-eight years. Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had been in that condition for a long time, so he asked him, “Do you want to be well?” The sick man answered him, “Sir, when the water is stirred up, there is no one to put me into the pool. And while I am on my way, someone else steps down before I do.” Jesus told him, “Get up, pick up your mat, and start walking.” Immediately the man became well. He picked up his mat and began walking about.

And this happened on a Sabbath. So the Jewish leaders kept telling the man who had been healed, “It is the Sabbath. It is against the law for you to carry your mat.” But he answered them, “The one who made me well is the one who told me, ‘Pick up your mat and start walking.’” So they asked him, “Who is this man who told you to pick it up and walk?” But the healed man had no idea who it was, since there was a crowd in the place and Jesus had moved off without being noticed. Afterward Jesus found him in the temple area and said to him, “Look, you are well now. Do not sin any longer, or something worse could come upon you.” The man went off and told the Jewish leaders that the one who had made him well was Jesus. For this reason the Jewish leaders began to persecute Jesus, since he kept doing such things on the Sabbath. Jesus answered them, “My Father has been at work right up to now, and I am at work as well.” So the Jewish leaders were even more determined to kill him. Besides breaking the Sabbath, he was speaking of God as his own Father, and so was making himself equal to God.

What the Son does

So Jesus gave them this answer: “Truly, truly, I tell you, the Son cannot do anything on his own; he does only what he sees the Father doing. For what the Father does, the Son does as well, and in the same way. For the Father loves the Son and shows him everything he himself is doing. And there are greater works than these that he will show him, so that you will be astonished. For the Father raises the dead and brings them to life, and in the same way the Son brings to life whomever he chooses. Nor does the Father judge anyone; he has given the whole work of judging to the Son, so that everyone will honor the Son just as they honor the Father. Whoever refuses honor to the Son refuses it to the Father who sent him.

Truly, truly, I tell you, anyone who hears my word and believes the one who sent me has eternal life. Such a person does not come under condemnation, but has already moved out of death into life.

Truly, truly, I tell you, an hour is coming, and in fact it has already begun, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear it will live. For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has given the Son life in himself as well. He has also given him authority to pass judgment, since he is the Son of Man. Do not be astonished at this. An hour is coming when everyone in the tombs will hear his voice and come out. Those who have done good will come out to a resurrection that brings life; those who have done evil, to a resurrection that brings condemnation.

I cannot do anything on my own. I judge according to what I hear, and the judgment I give is just, because I am not seeking to do my own will, but the will of the one who sent me.

Testimony about Jesus

If I testify on my own behalf, my testimony is not true. Someone else is testifying about me, and I know that the testimony he gives about me is true. You yourselves sent messengers to John, and he has testified to the truth. Yet I do not accept testimony from a human being; I say these things so that you may be saved. John was the lamp that burned and shone, and for a little while you were glad to rejoice in his light. But I have a testimony greater than John’s. The works the Father has given me to bring to completion, the works themselves that I am doing, testify about me: they show that the Father has sent me. And the Father who sent me has testified about me himself. Not once have you heard his voice or seen his form. And his word does not remain in you, since you do not believe the very one he sent.

You pore over the Scriptures, since you think that eternal life is to be found in them; and they are the ones that testify about me. But you do not want to come to me so that you can have life. Glory from people is not something I accept. But I know you, and there is no love for God in you. I have come in the name of my Father, yet you do not accept me. Should someone else come in his own name, him you will accept. How could you believe? You accept glory from one another, while the glory that comes from the only God is something you do not seek. Do not imagine that I will be the one to accuse you before the Father. You already have an accuser: Moses, in whom you have put your hope. If you really believed Moses, you would believe me, because what he wrote was about me. But if you do not believe the writings of Moses, how will you ever believe my spoken words?”

fields.title: John 6
fields.body_html:
Jesus feeds five thousand

Some time later Jesus went away across the Sea of Galilee, which is also called the Sea of Tiberias. A large crowd kept following him, because they kept seeing the signs he was doing by healing the sick. Jesus climbed up into the hills and sat there with his disciples. It was nearly time for Passover, the Jewish festival. Jesus looked up and saw that a large crowd was making its way toward him. So he asked Philip, “Where are we going to buy bread to feed these people?” Jesus said this to test Philip; he already knew what he was going to do. Philip answered him, “Bread costing more than half a year’s wages would not go far enough to give each of them even a little.” Then Andrew, one of his disciples and the brother of Simon Peter, said to him, “There is a young boy here who has five loaves of barley bread and two small fish. But what good is that with so many people?” Jesus said, “Tell the people to sit down.” Grass grew thickly in that spot. So the men sat down, about 5,000 of them. So Jesus took the loaves, gave thanks, and shared them out among the people sitting there, and the fish too, as much as anyone wanted. Once they were all full, he told his disciples, “Pick up the broken pieces that remain, so that nothing is lost.” They did so, and from the five barley loaves they filled twelve baskets with the pieces that remained after everyone had eaten. The people who had seen the sign he did kept saying, “This really is the Prophet, the one who is coming into the world!” Jesus realized that they were about to come and carry him off to make him king, so he went back up into the hills, alone.

Jesus walks on the sea

At evening his disciples went down to the shore. They boarded a boat and were making their way over the sea to Capernaum. Darkness had already fallen, and still Jesus had not come out to them. The sea was getting rough, whipped up by a strong wind. After they had rowed about 3 or 3½ miles, they caught sight of Jesus walking on the sea and getting close to the boat, and fear took hold of them. But he told them, “It is I. Do not be afraid.” Now they wanted to take him into the boat, and right away the boat arrived at the land they were heading for.

The bread of life

The next day the crowd that had stayed on the other side of the sea saw that there had been only one boat there, and that Jesus had not gone on board with his disciples. The disciples had left by themselves. Some boats from Tiberias, however, came in near the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord gave thanks. So when the crowd saw that neither Jesus nor his disciples were there, they got into the boats and went to Capernaum to look for him.

When they found him on the other side of the sea, they asked him, “Rabbi, when did you get here?” Jesus answered them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, you are looking for me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves. Do not work for food that passes away, but for the food that remains for eternal life, the food the Son of Man will give you. For he is the one God the Father has marked with his seal.” So they asked him, “What are we to do, to be doing the works that God asks of us?” Jesus answered them, “This is the work of God: that you believe in the one he sent.” So they said to him, “Then what sign will you perform for us to see, so that we will believe you? What work are you doing? Our ancestors ate the manna in the wilderness; as it is written, ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat.’” Jesus told them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, Moses was not the one who gave you the bread from heaven; my Father is the one who gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is the one that comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.” Then they said to him, “Sir, give us this bread all the time.”

Jesus said to them, “I am the bread of life. Those who come to me will never be hungry, and those who believe in me will never at any time be thirsty. But I said it already: you have seen me, yet you do not believe. Everyone the Father gives me will come to me, and I will never send away anyone who comes to me. For I have come down from heaven not to carry out my own will, but the will of the one who sent me. And the will of the one who sent me is this: that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it all up on the last day. For what my Father wills is this: everyone who sees the Son and believes in him will have eternal life, and I myself will raise them up on the last day.”

Then the Jews started grumbling about him, because he had claimed, “I am the bread that came down from heaven.” They kept saying, “Surely this is Jesus, the son of Joseph? We know his father and mother. So what does he mean by saying now, ‘I have come down from heaven’?” Jesus answered them, “Stop your grumbling to one another. Nobody can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws them. And on the last day I will raise them up. In the Prophets it is written, ‘They will all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard the Father’s teaching and learned it comes to me. This does not mean that anyone has seen the Father. Only the one who has come from God has seen him. Truly, truly, I tell you, anyone who believes has eternal life. I am the bread of life. Your ancestors ate the manna in the wilderness, and yet they died. Here, by contrast, is bread coming down from heaven: whoever eats it will not die. I am the living bread, come down from heaven. If anyone eats this bread, they will live forever. The bread I will give is my flesh, and I give it so that the world may have life.”

At this the Jews began to quarrel fiercely among themselves. “How can he give us his flesh to eat?” they said. Jesus answered them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, if you do not eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, there is no life in you. Anyone who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and on the last day I will raise them up. For my flesh is genuine food, and my blood is genuine drink. Anyone who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I remain in them. The living Father sent me, and I live because of him; in the same way, anyone who feeds on me will live because of me. This, then, is the bread that came down from heaven. It is not like the food the ancestors ate, for they died; anyone who eats this bread will live forever.” All this he said as he taught in the synagogue in Capernaum.

Many disciples turn back

When they heard this, many of his disciples said, “This message is harsh. Who can bear to listen to it?” Jesus was aware that his disciples were grumbling about this, so he said to them, “Does this make you stumble? Then what if you were to see the Son of Man going up to where he was before? The Spirit is the one who gives life; the flesh is of no benefit at all. The words I have spoken to you are spirit, and they are life. Yet some among you do not believe.” For Jesus had known from the start who the ones were that did not believe, and who would be the one to betray him. And he added, “This is the reason I told you that no one is able to come to me unless it has been given to them by the Father.”

At this, many of his disciples drew back and stopped going about with him. So Jesus asked the Twelve, “Surely you do not want to leave as well?” Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom would we go? You have words that bring eternal life. We have believed, and we know, that you are the Holy One of God.” Jesus answered them, “Did I not choose the twelve of you myself? Still, one of you is a devil.” He meant Judas, son of Simon Iscariot. Judas was one of the Twelve, and he was going to betray him.

fields.title: John 7
fields.body_html:
Jesus and his brothers

After this Jesus went from place to place in Galilee. He did not want to travel around Judea, because the Jewish leaders there were looking for a way to kill him. Now the Jewish Festival of Tabernacles was near. So his brothers said to him, “Leave this place and go to Judea, so that your disciples there can also see the works you are doing. No one who wants to be known openly does things in secret. If you are doing these things, show yourself to the world.” For even his own brothers did not believe in him. So the temple police returned to the chief priests and Pharisees, and these men asked them, “Why have you not brought him?” The temple police answered, “No one has ever spoken like this!” The Pharisees retorted, “Surely you have not been taken in as well? Jesus spoke to them once more: “I am the light of the world. Once more he said to them, “I am going away, and you will search for me, and you will die in your sin. fields.title: John 9
fields.body_html:
Jesus heals a man born blind

As Jesus was passing by, he saw a man who had been blind from birth. His disciples asked him, “Rabbi, who sinned, so that this man was born blind? Was it he, or his parents?” Jesus answered, “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents. It was so that the works of God might be made visible in him. While it is still day, we have to do the works of the one who sent me. Night is on its way, and then no one can work. While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” When he had said this, he spat on the ground, made mud with the saliva, and spread the mud on the man’s eyes. Then he told him, “Go and wash in the pool of Siloam” (the name means Sent). So the man went and washed, and he came back able to see. His neighbors, and others who had seen him earlier as a beggar, began asking, “Is this not the man who sat begging?” Some said, “That is the man.” Others said, “No, it is someone who looks like him.” The man himself kept saying, “I am the one.” So they asked him, “How were your eyes opened?” He answered, “The man named Jesus made mud and spread it on my eyes. He told me, ‘Go to Siloam and wash.’ So I went off and washed, and I began to see.” They asked him, “Where is he?” “I do not know,” he said.

The Pharisees question the man

They took the man who had been blind to the Pharisees. Now it was on a Sabbath that Jesus had made the mud and opened his eyes. So the Pharisees in turn asked him how he had gained his sight. He told them, “He put mud on my eyes, I washed, and I can see now.” Then some of the Pharisees said, “This man does not come from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath.” But others said, “How could a sinful man do signs like these?” And they were divided. So they questioned the man who had been blind once more: “And you, what do you say about him, since it was your eyes he opened?” He answered, “He is a prophet.”

The Jewish leaders did not believe that he had been blind and had gained his sight, until they summoned the parents of the man who could now see. They asked them, “Is this your son, the one you say was born blind? So how is he able to see now?” His parents answered, “We know he is our son, and we know he was born blind. But how he can see now, we do not know, and we do not know who opened his eyes. Ask him. He is of age and can answer for himself.” His parents spoke in this way out of fear of the Jewish leaders, who had already agreed that anyone who confessed him as the Christ would be expelled from the synagogue. This was why his parents said, “He is of age. Question him.”

So they summoned the man who had been blind a second time and said to him, “Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner.” He answered, “Whether he is a sinner, I do not know. I do know one thing: I used to be blind, and now I can see.” Then they asked him, “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?” He answered them, “I have told you already, and you would not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? Could it be that you want to become his disciples as well?” They insulted him and said, “You are a disciple of that man, but we are disciples of Moses. We know that God has spoken to Moses. Where this man comes from, we do not know.” The man answered them, “Well, here is something to wonder at: you do not know where he comes from, and still he opened my eyes! We know that God does not listen to sinners. But if someone reveres God and does his will, he listens to them. In all the ages, no one has ever heard of anyone opening the eyes of someone born blind. If this man were not from God, he would not be able to do anything at all.” They answered him, “You were born in sin through and through, and now you are teaching us?” And they threw him out.

Those who see and those who are blind

Jesus heard that they had thrown the man out, and when he found him, he said, “Do you believe in the Son of Man?” The man answered, “Who is he, Sir? Tell me, so that I may believe in him.” Jesus said to him, “You have seen him; he is the one who is speaking with you.” He said, “I believe, Lord.” And he worshiped him. Jesus said, “I came into this world to bring judgment, so that those who cannot see will see, and those who see will become blind.” Some of the Pharisees who were with him heard this and said to him, “You do not mean that we are blind too, do you?” Jesus said to them, “If you were blind, you would have no sin. But you say, ‘We can see,’ so your sin remains.”

So the Pharisees in turn asked him how he had gained his sight. He told them, “He put mud on my eyes, I washed, and I can see now.” Then some of the Pharisees said, “This man does not come from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath.” But others said, “How could a sinful man do signs like these?” And they were divided. fields.title: John 10
fields.body_html:
The shepherd and the sheep

“Truly, truly, I tell you, anyone who does not go into the sheepfold by the door, but climbs in from somewhere else, is a thief and a bandit. But the one who goes in through the door is the shepherd of the sheep. For him the doorkeeper opens the door, and the sheep hear his voice. He calls each of his own sheep by name and leads them out. Once he has brought all his own sheep out, he walks on ahead, and the sheep follow him because they know his voice. They will not follow a stranger at all. They will run from him, because they do not know the voices of strangers.” Jesus spoke this figure of speech to them, but they did not grasp what he meant by it.

So Jesus spoke to them again: “Truly, truly, I tell you, I am the door for the sheep. All who came before me are thieves and bandits, but the sheep did not give them a hearing. I am the door. If anyone goes in through me, they will be saved, going in and going out and finding pasture. The thief comes for no other reason than to steal and slaughter and destroy. I came so that they may have life, and have it in overflowing measure.

The good shepherd

I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. A hired man is no shepherd, and the sheep are not his own. So when he sees the wolf coming, he leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf seizes them and scatters the flock. He flees because he works only for pay, and the sheep mean nothing to him. I am the good shepherd. I know those who are mine, and those who are mine know me, just as the Father knows me and I know the Father. And I lay down my life for the sheep. I have other sheep as well, which are not of this fold. I must bring them too, and they will listen to my voice, and they will become one flock with one shepherd. This is why the Father loves me: because I lay down my life in order to take it up again. No one takes it from me; I lay it down of my own accord. I have authority to lay it down, and authority to take it up again. This is the command I received from my Father.”

Divided over Jesus

Once more the Jews who were listening were divided because of these words. Many of them said, “He has a demon and is out of his mind. Why listen to him?” Others said, “This is not how a man with a demon speaks. Surely a demon cannot open the eyes of the blind?” Then came the time of the Feast of Dedication in Jerusalem. It was winter, and Jesus was walking about in the temple courts, in Solomon’s Colonnade. So the Jews who were there surrounded him and said to him, “How long will you leave us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us in plain words.” Jesus answered them, “I have told you, and you do not believe. The works I do in my Father’s name are themselves witnesses for me. But you do not believe, because you are not among my sheep. The sheep that belong to me listen to my voice; I know them, and they follow me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one will snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who gave them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand. The Father and I are one.”

The charge of blasphemy

Once more the Jews who had gathered around him picked up stones to stone him. Jesus said to them, “I have shown you many good works that come from the Father. Which of those works are you trying to stone me for?” The Jews answered him, “It is not because of a good work that we are stoning you. It is because of blasphemy: you are only a man, and you are making yourself God.” Jesus answered them, “Your own law says, does it not, ‘I said, “You are gods”‘? If he called them gods, the people to whom the word of God came, and Scripture cannot be broken, how can you tell him, the one whom the Father set apart and sent into the world, ‘You are blaspheming,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’? If I am not doing my Father’s works, do not believe me. But if I am doing them, then even if you do not believe me, believe the works. Then you will come to know, and go on knowing, that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.” So once more they tried to arrest him, but he slipped out of their hands.

Across the Jordan

Then Jesus went back across the Jordan to the place where John had been baptizing in the early days, and he stayed there. Many people came to him. “John did not do a single sign,” they said, “but every word John spoke about this man was true.” And many people there believed in him.

fields.title: John 11
fields.body_html:
The death of Lazarus

A certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, the village where Mary lived with her sister Martha. Mary was the one who anointed the Lord with perfumed oil and wiped his feet with her hair, and Lazarus, who was ill, was her brother. The sisters therefore sent him a message: “Lord, look, the one you love is ill.” When Jesus heard this, he said, “This illness is not going to end in death; it is for the sake of God’s glory, so that through it the Son of God may be glorified.” Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed where he was for two more days. Then, after that, he said to the disciples, “Let us go back to Judea.” The disciples said to him, “Rabbi, only just now the Jews at the temple were seeking to stone you, and you are going there again?” Jesus answered, “Does the day not have twelve hours? Whoever walks in daylight does not stumble, because they see the light of this world. But whoever walks at night stumbles, because the light is not in them.” After he had said this, he told them, “Lazarus, our friend, has fallen asleep, but I am setting out to wake him.” The disciples replied, “Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will get well.” Jesus, however, had been speaking about the death of Lazarus. They thought he was talking about ordinary sleep. Then Jesus told them in plain words, “Lazarus has died. I am glad for your sakes that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him.” Then Thomas, also called Didymus (which means Twin), said to the other disciples, “Let us go too, so that we may die with him.”

The resurrection and the life

When Jesus came, he found that Lazarus had been in the tomb four days already. Bethany was near Jerusalem, about 2 miles away. Many Jews had come to Martha and Mary to comfort them over the loss of their brother. When Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went out to meet him, while Mary stayed sitting in the house. Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, had you been here, my brother would not have died. Even now I know that God will give you anything you ask him for.” Jesus told her, “Your brother will rise again.” Martha answered, “I know he will rise when the dead are raised, on the last day.” Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even if they die, will live, and all who live and believe in me will never die. Do you believe this?” She answered, “Yes, Lord. I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of God, the one who is coming into the world.”

Jesus raises Lazarus

When she had said this, she went back and called her sister Mary aside privately. “The Teacher is here,” she said, “and he is calling for you.” As soon as Mary heard this, she got up quickly and went to him. Jesus had not yet come into the village; he was still at the place where Martha had met him. The Jews who were with Mary in the house, comforting her, saw her get up quickly and go out. They followed her, thinking that she was going to the tomb to weep there. When Mary reached the place where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet and said to him, “Lord, had you been here, my brother would not have died.” When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her weeping too, he was deeply indignant in spirit and greatly troubled. “Where have you laid him?” he asked. They said to him, “Lord, come and see.” Jesus wept. So the Jews who were there said, “See how much he loved him!” But some of them said, “He opened the eyes of the blind man. Was he not able to keep this man from dying as well?” Jesus, once more deeply indignant within himself, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay over the entrance. Jesus said, “Take the stone away.” Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him, “Lord, he already stinks; this is the fourth day.” Jesus said to her, “Did I not tell you that you would see the glory of God if you believed?” So they took the stone away. Then Jesus raised his eyes upward and said, “Father, I give you thanks that you have heard me. I myself knew that you hear me at all times. But I have spoken for the sake of the crowd standing around, so that they may believe that it was you who sent me.” After these words he cried out with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!” Out came the man who had been dead, with his feet and hands bound in strips of cloth and a cloth tied around his face. Jesus told them, “Untie him and let him go.”

The plot to kill Jesus

Many of the Jews who had come to Mary, and had seen what he did, believed in him. Some of them, however, went off to the Pharisees and reported what Jesus had done. So the chief priests and the Pharisees called a meeting of the council. “What are we doing?” they said. “This man is doing many signs. If we leave him alone, everyone will end up believing in him. Then the Romans will come and take from us both our holy place and our nation.” One of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, “You do not know anything! You have not worked out that it is to your advantage to have one man die for the people, instead of the whole nation perishing.” Caiaphas did not say this on his own. Because he was high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus was going to die for the nation, and not for the nation alone, but also to bring God’s scattered children together into one. So from that day on they plotted together to kill him.

So Jesus stopped moving about in public among the Jews of Judea. He left and went to the countryside near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and stayed there with his disciples.

The Passover draws near

It was nearly time for the Jewish Passover. Many people from the countryside went up to Jerusalem before the festival to make themselves ritually clean. They kept looking for Jesus, and as they stood in the temple courts they asked one another, “What do you think? Will he not come to the festival at all?” Meanwhile the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that anyone who knew where Jesus was must report it, so that they could arrest him.

fields.title: John 12
fields.body_html:
Mary anoints Jesus

Then, six days before the Passover, Jesus arrived in Bethany, where Lazarus was, the man Jesus had raised from the dead. So they gave a dinner for him there. Martha was serving, and Lazarus was one of the guests who reclined at table with him. Then Mary took about 12 ounces of very costly perfumed oil, pure nard, and anointed Jesus’s feet and wiped his feet with her hair. The fragrance of the oil filled the house. But one of his disciples spoke up: Judas Iscariot, who was soon to betray him. “Why was this oil not sold for about a year’s wages and the money given to the poor?” He said this, not out of any care for the poor, but because he was a thief. He was in charge of the money box, and he used to take for himself what people put in it. Jesus said, “Leave her alone. She was to keep it for the day when my body is prepared for burial. There will always be poor people among you, but I will not always be with you.”

When a large crowd of the Jews learned that Jesus was there, they came, not only for Jesus’s sake; they wanted to see Lazarus as well, the man he had raised from the dead. The chief priests, however, resolved to put Lazarus to death as well, because on his account many of the Jews were leaving them and believing in Jesus.

The king comes to Jerusalem

The next day the large crowd that had come for the festival heard that Jesus was on his way into Jerusalem. They took branches from the palm trees and went out to meet him. They were shouting, “Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord, Israel’s King!” Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it, just as Scripture says: “Do not be afraid, daughter of Zion! Look, your king is coming, sitting on a donkey’s colt.” At first his disciples did not understand what these things meant. But when Jesus had been glorified, they remembered that these things had been written about him, and that they had done these very things for him. Meanwhile the crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus out of his tomb and raised him from the dead kept on testifying to what they had seen. That was also why the crowd went out to meet him: they had heard that he had done this sign. So the Pharisees said to one another, “You can see for yourselves that you are getting nowhere. Look, the whole world has gone off after him!”

The hour has come

Among those who went up to worship at the festival were some Greeks. These men came to Philip, whose home was Bethsaida in Galilee, and made a request of him: “Sir, we would like to see Jesus.” Philip went and told Andrew, and then Andrew and Philip went and told Jesus. Jesus answered them, “The hour has come when the Son of Man is to be glorified. Truly, truly, I tell you, if a grain of wheat does not fall into the ground and die, it stays just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. Whoever loves their life is losing it, and whoever hates their life in this world will keep it safe for eternal life. Anyone who serves me must follow me, and my servant will be where I am. The Father will honor anyone who serves me.

Now my soul is troubled, and what should I say? Father, save me from this hour. But it was for this very reason that I came to this hour. Father, glorify your name.” Then a voice came out of heaven: “I have glorified it and will glorify it again.” The crowd that stood there and heard it said it had thundered. Others were saying, “An angel has spoken to him.” Jesus answered, “This voice came for your sake, not for mine. Now is the time of judgment for this world; now the ruler of this world will be driven out. As for me, when I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all people to myself.” He said this to show what kind of death he was going to die. The crowd answered him, “We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever. So how can you tell us that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?” So Jesus told them, “The light is among you for only a little while longer. Walk while you have the light, so that darkness does not overtake you. Anyone who walks in the darkness does not know where they are going. While you have the light, believe in the light, and so become children of light.”

Why many did not believe

When Jesus had said these things, he went away and hid himself from them. Although Jesus had done so many signs before their eyes, they did not believe in him. It happened this way so that the word the prophet Isaiah spoke would be fulfilled: “Lord, who has believed our message? And to whom has the Lord’s arm been revealed?” This is why they could not believe, because in another place Isaiah said: “He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they would not see with their eyes, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I would heal them.” Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke about him. Even so, many even among the rulers believed in him. But because of the Pharisees they would not say so openly, so that they would not be expelled from the synagogue. For they loved the glory that people give more than the glory that God gives. Then Jesus called out, “Anyone who believes in me believes not just in me, but in the one who sent me. And anyone who sees me sees the one who sent me. I have come as a light into the world, so that whoever believes in me will not remain in the darkness. If anyone hears my words but does not keep them, I do not condemn them. For I did not come to condemn the world, but to save the world. Anyone who rejects me and does not accept my words has a judge: the very word I have spoken will judge them on the last day. For I have not spoken on my own authority; the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment about what to say and what to speak. And I know that his commandment is eternal life. So whatever I say, I say just as the Father has told me.”
